course.title: Psychotherapy
course.desc: Session notes, treatment plans, psychoeducation, case conceptualization.

exercises.title: Vague vs. precise
exercises.sc:
You just finished a 50-minute session with a client experiencing complicated grief after losing a spouse. You need to write a clinical note. Most therapists type something like:

"Summarize this session."

The AI returns a generic paragraph that misses the clinical details your supervisor and insurance reviewer actually need.
exercises.task: Write a better prompt. Be specific about: what clinical elements to capture (presenting problem, interventions used, client affect, homework assigned), what format you want, and what details to highlight for continuity of care.
exercises.hint: A 200-word specification like 'summarize the session focusing on grief processing interventions, client's emotional regulation, and progress toward treatment goals' beats 'summarize this session' followed by 15 corrections.
exercises.cr: 1) Specifies which clinical elements to capture (interventions, affect, risk factors) 2) Defines output format (SOAP, DAP, or narrative) 3) Mentions what to highlight for treatment continuity 4) Is substantially more detailed than 'summarize this session'

exercises.title: Specify the output
exercises.sc: Your clinic director asks you to "get the AI to score and interpret this client's assessment battery." You have PHQ-9, GAD-7, and PCL-5 scores from an intake evaluation, plus demographic information and referral reason.
exercises.task: Write a prompt that specifies exactly what the output should look like. Define the structure — severity table? Clinical interpretation paragraphs? What scores, cutoffs, and cross-measure patterns should be included?
exercises.hint: If you handed the output to a prescribing psychiatrist, would they immediately understand the clinical picture without follow-up questions?
exercises.cr: 1) Specifies output format explicitly (table, narrative, or both) 2) Names specific scoring instruments and their cutoffs 3) Requests cross-measure interpretation 4) Defines what a clinically useful summary looks like

exercises.title: Audience and tone
exercises.sc:
A 34-year-old client diagnosed with Generalized Anxiety Disorder needs psychoeducation about their condition. You need to communicate essentially the same information to three different audiences:

1. The client (warm, accessible, empowering)
2. A referring physician (clinical, concise)
3. A disability insurance reviewer (formal, evidence-based)
exercises.task: Write a prompt for ONE audience that explicitly controls tone, length, and emphasis. Make it clear who the reader is and what they care about.
exercises.hint: The client wants to understand 'why do I feel this way and what can I do?' The physician wants diagnostic clarity and treatment response. The insurance reviewer wants functional impairment and medical necessity.
exercises.cr: 1) Clearly identifies target audience 2) Specifies tone appropriate to that audience 3) Defines what to emphasize vs. omit 4) Sets length expectations 5) Shows audience-aware clinical framing

exercises.title: Setting constraints
exercises.sc: You're asking the AI to draft an individual treatment plan for a client with Major Depressive Disorder, recurrent, moderate (F33.1). Without constraints, the AI produces either a vague two-paragraph plan or a 10-page document with interventions you don't use and goals that aren't measurable.
exercises.task: Write a prompt with explicit constraints: session frequency and duration limits from the insurance authorization, required sections (problems, goals, objectives, interventions), measurable objective format, and what NOT to include.
exercises.hint: Telling the AI 'do not include pharmacotherapy recommendations — I am not a prescriber' is just as valuable as telling it what to include.
exercises.cr: 1) Sets specific session/timeline constraints from insurance authorization 2) Includes 'do not' instructions (e.g., no prescribing recommendations) 3) Lists required treatment plan sections 4) Specifies measurable objective format 5) Demonstrates negative constraints relevant to scope of practice

exercises.title: Role assignment
exercises.sc: You want the AI to review your case conceptualization for a client presenting with both trauma symptoms and substance use. You could just say "review this case conceptualization" — but the feedback depends entirely on what clinical lens the AI uses.
exercises.task: Write a prompt that assigns the AI a specific clinical role (e.g., "You are a licensed clinical supervisor with 20 years of experience in trauma-informed care and dual diagnosis treatment"). Define what expertise and theoretical orientation to apply.
exercises.hint: A psychodynamic supervisor flags different things than a CBT-oriented one. A trauma specialist catches what a generalist misses.
exercises.cr: 1) Assigns a specific clinical role with credentials and specialization 2) Defines what theoretical orientation to apply 3) Specifies what to evaluate in the case conceptualization 4) Role choice meaningfully shapes the clinical feedback

exercises.title: Iterative refinement
exercises.sc:
You asked the AI for a therapy progress note and got:

"Client attended session and discussed anxiety. Therapist provided supportive counseling. Client reports feeling somewhat better. Will continue treatment."

This is clinically useless — no specific interventions, no measurable observations, no treatment plan linkage. Your supervisor would send this back immediately.
exercises.task: Write a follow-up prompt that fixes this. Don't start over — refine. Tell the AI specifically what's wrong and what clinical detail to add.
exercises.hint: Good refinement is surgical: 'Add the specific CBT intervention used (cognitive restructuring of catastrophic thinking about job loss), the client's subjective distress rating (dropped from 7/10 to 4/10), and link progress to Treatment Goal #2.' Bad: 'Make it more clinical.'
exercises.cr: 1) References specific problems in the original note 2) Gives targeted clinical corrections 3) Adds missing specifics (interventions, scores, observations) 4) Shows refinement over restarting 5) Demonstrates the iterate-and-improve cycle

exercises.title: Plan before you ask
exercises.sc:
You need a comprehensive treatment protocol specification for a new intensive outpatient program (IOP) for adults with treatment-resistant depression. If you just say "write a treatment protocol," you'll get a generic document that doesn't meet accreditation standards or reflect your program's modality mix.

The principle: spend 10 minutes planning the prompt to save an hour of corrections.
exercises.task: Write a detailed specification prompt (150-250 words). Include: program philosophy, target population criteria, required protocol sections, session structure, outcome measures, evidence base requirements, and exclusions.
exercises.hint: Your specification IS the prompt. The more precise the treatment protocol spec, the better the first output — think CARF or Joint Commission standards.
exercises.cr: 1) Defines program philosophy and target population 2) Lists specific protocol sections 3) Specifies evidence-based modalities to include 4) Sets outcome measurement requirements 5) Includes exclusions and contraindications 6) Spec itself is 100+ words

exercises.title: Chain-of-thought
exercises.sc: A new client was referred after a psychiatric emergency department visit. You have their intake paperwork, self-report measures, and a brief referral note. You need to conduct a thorough risk assessment before the first session.
exercises.task: Write a prompt forcing step-by-step clinical reasoning: first extract risk factors from the materials, then categorize them (static vs. dynamic, acute vs. chronic), then weigh protective factors, then assign a risk level with justification. Use explicit step numbering.
exercises.hint: Chain-of-thought: 'Before giving your risk determination, first list all identified risk factors, then categorize each as static or dynamic, then list protective factors, then reason through the overall picture.' Sequential clinical reasoning catches what gut reactions miss.
exercises.cr: 1) Uses explicit numbered steps for clinical reasoning 2) Separates data extraction from clinical judgment 3) Asks for reasoning before conclusions 4) Includes risk categorization system (static/dynamic, acute/chronic) 5) Steps build logically toward a defensible risk determination

exercises.title: Few-shot examples
exercises.sc:
You're training the AI to identify cognitive distortions in client statements — a core CBT skill. You want it to reliably categorize distortions across different client presentations.

Examples:
• "I failed one exam, so I'll never succeed at anything" → All-or-Nothing Thinking + Overgeneralization
• "I know my boss thinks I'm incompetent" → Mind Reading
• "If I go to the party, something terrible will happen" → Catastrophizing + Fortune Telling
exercises.task: Write a prompt using few-shot examples that teaches the AI to identify cognitive distortions in new client statements. Include examples in consistent format, define all distortion categories, and add 2-3 test cases for the AI to classify.
exercises.hint: Format consistency matters: if examples use '→', use '→' for all. Include the full list of common cognitive distortions (Beck's original list) so the AI has the complete taxonomy.
exercises.cr: 1) Includes 3+ clear example pairs with distortion labels 2) Defines all cognitive distortion categories 3) Examples cover multiple distortion types 4) Includes new client statements as test cases 5) Consistent format throughout

exercises.title: Structured output
exercises.sc: Your client with PTSD and comorbid depression needs a structured safety plan. Instead of a wall of text, you want a formatted document the client can actually use during a crisis — something they can keep on their phone or refrigerator.
exercises.task: Write a prompt that enforces a specific safety plan structure. Define exact sections (warning signs, coping strategies, people to contact, professional resources, means restriction steps), what goes in each, and how to handle sections the client hasn't filled in yet.
exercises.hint: Show the exact format you want. A safety plan that looks like the Stanley-Brown Safety Planning Intervention format is more clinically useful than a narrative paragraph.
exercises.cr: 1) Defines exact safety plan structure with all required sections 2) Explains what content belongs in each section 3) Uses a recognized safety planning format 4) Handles incomplete information gracefully 5) Optionally includes an example entry per section

exercises.title: Compare and evaluate
exercises.sc:
A client with chronic pain and comorbid anxiety is asking about therapy options. You want to present an evidence-based comparison. Three modalities are on the table:

A: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) — structured, goal-oriented, strong evidence base
B: Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) — emotion regulation focus, skills-based
C: Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) — psychological flexibility, values-based
exercises.task: Write a prompt that evaluates all three approaches against specific criteria relevant to this client's presentation. Define 3-4 criteria, ask for per-criterion ratings, and require a justified recommendation based on the client's specific needs.
exercises.hint: Don't ask 'which therapy is best?' Instead: 'Rate each 1-5 on evidence for chronic pain, evidence for anxiety, client engagement demands, and time-to-benefit, given that the client has limited distress tolerance and prefers structured approaches.'
exercises.cr: 1) Defines 3+ clinically relevant comparison criteria 2) Asks for per-criterion ratings or scores 3) Requires clinical reasoning for each rating 4) Requests a justified recommendation tailored to this client 5) Criteria are meaningful and non-overlapping

exercises.title: Multi-step decomposition
exercises.sc: A new client is coming in for an intake assessment. They were referred by their PCP for "depression and possible ADHD." You need to complete a comprehensive biopsychosocial intake, but the full process is too complex for one prompt — history gathering, symptom assessment, diagnostic formulation, and treatment recommendations all require different approaches.
exercises.task: Write a SEQUENCE of 3-4 prompts that decompose the intake assessment process. Each builds on the previous output. Show the full chain from information gathering through diagnostic impression to initial treatment plan.
exercises.hint: Workflow: Gather history → Organize symptoms by DSM-5 criteria → Formulate differential diagnosis → Develop initial treatment recommendations. Each step has clear clinical input and output.
exercises.cr: 1) Breaks into 3+ sequential prompts 2) Each has a focused clinical objective 3) Later prompts reference earlier clinical outputs 4) Covers data gathering → assessment → diagnosis → planning 5) Demonstrates decomposition of complex clinical workflow

exercises.title: Error correction
exercises.sc:
The AI produced this clinical assessment summary:

"Client presents with depression, likely caused by recent divorce. Diagnosis: Major Depressive Disorder. Recommend weekly CBT for 12 sessions."

Problems: single-factor etiology, jumped to diagnosis without differential, assumed treatment modality without considering client factors, no severity specifier, no rule-outs.
exercises.task: Write a prompt correcting these clinical reasoning errors. Ask for biopsychosocial formulation, differential diagnosis with rule-outs, severity assessment, and treatment recommendations that consider client preferences and comorbidities.
exercises.hint: Point out exactly what's wrong: 'You attributed depression solely to the divorce without considering biological factors, trauma history, substance use, or medical conditions. You skipped differential diagnosis entirely.'
exercises.cr: 1) Identifies specific clinical reasoning errors 2) Asks for biopsychosocial formulation rather than single-factor explanation 3) Addresses missing differential diagnosis 4) Requests severity specifiers and rule-outs 5) Shows critical clinical thinking

exercises.title: Persona prompting
exercises.sc:
A complex case needs multidisciplinary review: a 16-year-old with self-harm behaviors, family conflict, declining grades, and a recent ADHD diagnosis. You want to stress-test your treatment approach from three clinical perspectives:

1. Consulting psychiatrist (medication considerations, diagnostic clarity)
2. School social worker (academic impact, IEP/504 accommodations)
3. Family therapist (family systems dynamics, parent coaching)
exercises.task: Write a prompt that has the AI adopt each clinical persona sequentially, review the case from their expertise, then synthesize into a unified multidisciplinary treatment recommendation.
exercises.hint: Each persona surfaces different concerns. The psychiatrist asks about medication interactions and diagnostic accuracy. The social worker focuses on school functioning and support systems. The family therapist looks at family dynamics maintaining the problem.
exercises.cr: 1) Defines 3 distinct clinical personas with specific expertise 2) Each has domain-specific concerns 3) Sequential analysis from each perspective 4) Requests synthesis into unified recommendations 5) Shows how clinical perspective shapes case conceptualization

exercises.title: Prompt templates
exercises.sc: You write SOAP notes after every therapy session — that's 20-30 per week. Instead of writing a new prompt each time, you want a reusable template that works for any client, any session, any modality.
exercises.task: Create a reusable SOAP note prompt template with [BRACKET] variables. Include: client identifier, session number, presenting problem, interventions used, modality, outcome measures, and next session plan. Should work for any session with any client.
exercises.hint: Variables like [CLIENT_ID], [SESSION_NUMBER], [PRIMARY_MODALITY], [INTERVENTION_LIST], [SUBJECTIVE_DISTRESS_RATING] make it reusable — fill in the blanks and get a consistent, billable note every time.
exercises.cr: 1) Uses clear bracket variables for session-specific data 2) Genuinely reusable across clients and modalities 3) Covers all SOAP sections (Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan) 4) 4+ variable placeholders 5) Would save significant documentation time

exercises.title: Case conceptualization
exercises.sc: You have a complex client: 42-year-old woman presenting with panic attacks, agoraphobia, and a history of childhood emotional neglect. She's been through two previous therapists without improvement. Your supervisor wants a thorough case conceptualization before your next supervision meeting.
exercises.task: Write a prompt producing a structured case conceptualization: predisposing factors, precipitating factors, perpetuating factors, protective factors (the 4 P's), a theoretical formulation linking history to current symptoms, and treatment implications.
exercises.hint: Structure your prompt like a clinical framework: gather the pieces (4 P's), connect them through your theoretical lens, then derive treatment targets. A good conceptualization explains WHY this client has THESE symptoms at THIS time.
exercises.cr: 1) Addresses all 4 P's (predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating, protective) 2) Requests a theoretical formulation linking factors 3) Specifies output structure 4) Includes treatment implications derived from the formulation 5) Covers the presenting problem comprehensively 6) Professional clinical output

exercises.title: Waitlist triage
exercises.sc: Your community mental health clinic has 43 people on the waitlist and just lost a therapist. You need to prioritize who gets seen first based on clinical urgency, risk level, and wait time. Some are routine referrals, some flagged as urgent by their PCP.
exercises.task: Write a prompt that creates a triage system for waitlist prioritization. Define urgency tiers, risk criteria, required screening questions, and a scannable output format that front desk staff can use.
exercises.hint: Triage matrix: Acute risk (immediate) → Active crisis (within 48h) → Urgent clinical need (within 1 week) → Routine (standard wait). Include both clinical and practical factors.
exercises.cr: 1) Defines clear triage tiers with criteria 2) Specifies risk assessment factors 3) Distinguishes urgency levels with timeframes 4) Creates a scannable output format 5) Is practical for front desk and clinical staff to use

exercises.title: Group therapy notes
exercises.sc: You just facilitated a 90-minute DBT skills group with 8 participants. Topics covered: distress tolerance skills (TIPP, ACCEPTS), role-play exercises, homework review. Some members were highly engaged, one was disruptive, and another disclosed a crisis situation. You need structured group notes that capture both group dynamics and individual participation.
exercises.task: Write a prompt transforming your rough group session notes into structured documentation: group-level summary, individual member participation notes, skills taught, incidents requiring follow-up, and homework assignments.
exercises.hint: Template: Group Summary (theme, skills, dynamics) → Individual Notes (participation, affect, disclosures) → Clinical Alerts (risk, follow-up needed) → Next Session Plan.
exercises.cr: 1) Defines output sections for group documentation 2) Captures both group-level and individual-level data 3) Handles clinical incidents requiring follow-up 4) Prioritizes clinically relevant observations 5) Includes next session planning

exercises.title: Insurance comparison
exercises.sc:
A client needs to choose between three insurance plans for next year, and mental health coverage is their top priority. They're in weekly individual therapy, take two psychiatric medications, and may need psychological testing.

• Plan A: Aetna PPO ($420/mo, $1,500 deductible, 30% coinsurance after deductible)
• Plan B: Blue Cross HMO ($310/mo, $500 deductible, $40 copay per visit, requires referral)
• Plan C: United HSA ($280/mo, $3,000 deductible, 20% coinsurance, $500 employer HSA contribution)

Need a 12-month total cost comparison focused on mental health utilization.
exercises.task: Write a prompt for a structured mental health cost comparison: time horizon, all cost categories (premiums, deductibles, copays, medication costs, testing coverage), explicit assumptions about utilization, and recommendation format.
exercises.hint: Include: weekly therapy costs, monthly medication copays, one-time psych testing, out-of-network implications, deductible timing. State all assumptions about visit frequency and medication costs.
exercises.cr: 1) All mental health cost categories (therapy, meds, testing) 2) Clear 12-month timeframe 3) Explicit utilization assumptions 4) Summary comparison table 5) Recommendation with clinical reasoning 6) Network adequacy dimension

exercises.title: Program evaluation report
exercises.sc: Your clinic director wants a 5-page outcome evaluation report for the board of directors on your Trauma Recovery Program's first year. Data-driven, with clinical outcomes, client satisfaction, and recommendations for Year 2.
exercises.task: Write the specification prompt — the detailed brief for a board-ready program evaluation report on the first try. Structure, length per section, outcome data requirements, clinical metrics, tone, and exclusions.
exercises.hint: This is the ultimate 'plan before you ask' exercise. A 200-word spec produces a board-ready report. A 20-word instruction produces something you'll rewrite 15 times.
exercises.cr: 1) Defines report structure with sections 2) Length per section specified 3) Clinical outcome metrics required (pre-post scores, completion rates) 4) Board-appropriate tone 5) Exclusions stated 6) Spec is 150+ words 7) Would produce a professional program evaluation

exercises.title: Therapy termination comms
exercises.sc:
You need to terminate therapy with a client who has developed an unhealthy dependency on the therapeutic relationship and is not making progress toward treatment goals. The client has borderline personality features and a history of abandonment. You need:
1. A session script for the termination conversation
2. A referral letter to a new therapist
3. A clinical documentation note justifying the decision
exercises.task: Write one prompt producing all three documents with different tones but consistent clinical reasoning. Address the therapeutic sensitivity while maintaining professional boundaries.
exercises.hint: The session script must be warm and boundaried. The referral letter must be clinical and thorough. The documentation must be defensible. Facts identical across documents, framing changes per audience.
exercises.cr: 1) Requests all three documents 2) Different tones for each (therapeutic, clinical, legal/documentation) 3) Consistent clinical facts 4) Addresses abandonment sensitivity authentically 5) Handles ethical boundary considerations 6) Strategic clinical communication

exercises.title: Therapist credential review
exercises.sc: You're hiring a new therapist for your group practice specializing in trauma and eating disorders. Requirements: licensed (LCSW/LPC/PhD), 3+ years post-licensure, EMDR or CPT certified, experience with eating disorders, comfortable with DBT skills. 10 applications to screen, shortlist top 3.
exercises.task: Write a prompt creating systematic credential screening: scored criteria with weights, must-have vs nice-to-have qualifications, clinical red flags, and shortlist output format.
exercises.hint: Chain-of-thought: extract credentials → verify licensure requirements → score against clinical competencies → rank → recommend. Weighted scoring prevents hiring based on gut feel alone.
exercises.cr: 1) Scored criteria with weights for clinical competencies 2) Must-haves vs nice-to-haves clearly separated 3) Clinical red flags specific to therapy hiring 4) Comparison table output 5) Reasoning behind rankings 6) Multiple techniques combined

exercises.title: Treatment outcome analysis
exercises.sc:
Your practice has 12 months of outcome data: PHQ-9 and GAD-7 scores at intake and discharge for 85 clients across 4 therapists and 3 treatment modalities (CBT, EMDR, DBT). You also have client satisfaction surveys, dropout rates, and session utilization data. You need to:
1. Analyze clinical outcomes
2. Identify trends by therapist and modality
3. Prioritize quality improvement targets
4. Report to the clinical team and board
exercises.task: Write a comprehensive prompt for this end-to-end analysis pipeline. Use few-shot for outcome categorization (improved/no change/deteriorated), chain-of-thought for trend analysis, structured output for the report, and persona prompting for different audience sections.
exercises.hint: Capstone: combine every technique. Few-shot + structured output + chain-of-thought + planning + audience awareness. This is a real clinical operations task.
exercises.cr: 1) Few-shot examples for outcome categorization 2) Clear clinical outcome categories with cutoff scores 3) Trend identification by therapist and modality 4) Quality improvement prioritization criteria 5) Structured report for multiple audiences 6) 3+ techniques combined 7) Reusable clinical analytics workflow

materials.1:
SESSION TRANSCRIPT EXCERPT (Fictional Client: "Maria S.", Session #12)

Therapist: Last week we talked about the anniversary of David's passing coming up. How has this week been?

Client: Terrible, honestly. I couldn't even go to the grocery store we used to shop at together. I just sat in the parking lot and cried for twenty minutes. My daughter called and I didn't pick up because I didn't want her to hear me like that.

Therapist: That sounds like a really painful moment. I notice you mentioned avoiding the store and also avoiding your daughter's call. Can we look at what was happening in your body and mind in that parking lot?

Client: My chest got tight, and I kept thinking "I can't do this alone." It's been 14 months and I still can't buy groceries without falling apart.

Therapist: That thought — "I can't do this alone" — we've seen that pattern before. Last session we identified it as a core belief connected to your grief. Today I'd like us to try some cognitive restructuring around that. What's the evidence for and against that thought?

Client: I mean... I did drive there by myself. And I've been paying the bills and cooking dinner. But it doesn't feel like enough.

[Session continued with cognitive restructuring exercise, grounding techniques, and assignment of grief journaling homework. Client's SUDS decreased from 8/10 to 5/10 during session.]

materials.3:
CLIENT BACKGROUND (Fictional Client: "Priya K.")

Diagnosis: Generalized Anxiety Disorder (F41.1)
Age: 34, Female, Software Engineer
Duration of treatment: 8 sessions of CBT
Current medications: Sertraline 100mg (prescribed by psychiatrist Dr. Patel)

Symptom presentation:
- Chronic worry about work performance, health, family safety
- Physical symptoms: muscle tension, insomnia, GI distress
- GAD-7 score at intake: 16 (Severe)
- GAD-7 score at session 8: 11 (Moderate)
- Functional impairment: Missed 3 work days last month, avoids driving on highways

Treatment progress:
- Learned diaphragmatic breathing (uses daily)
- Cognitive restructuring: Can identify worry spirals, still struggles to reframe
- Behavioral: Completed 2 of 4 exposure hierarchy items
- Sleep improved from 4-5 hours to 6-7 hours with sleep hygiene protocol

Key information for different audiences:
- For client: What GAD is, why her brain does this, what she can do
- For physician: Treatment response, medication interaction, functional status
- For insurance: Medical necessity, symptom severity, functional impairment, treatment gains
materials.4:
TREATMENT PLAN CONTEXT (Fictional Client: "Robert M.")

Client: Robert M., 47-year-old male
Diagnosis: Major Depressive Disorder, Recurrent, Moderate (F33.1)
Insurance: Blue Cross PPO
Authorization: 16 sessions over 6 months, individual therapy
Session frequency: Weekly x 8 weeks, then biweekly x 8 weeks
Provider: Licensed Clinical Social Worker (LCSW)

Presenting problems:
- Persistent depressed mood (PHQ-9: 15, moderately severe)
- Social withdrawal — stopped attending church, gym, friend gatherings
- Occupational impairment — missed 6 days in past month, performance review warning
- Sleep disturbance — early morning awakening, 4-5 hours/night
- Loss of interest in previously enjoyed activities (fishing, cooking)

Client preferences:
- Open to therapy, resistant to medication discussion
- Prefers structured approach with homework
- Religious faith is important coping resource
- Previous therapy (3 sessions, 2019) — dropped out, "didn't feel helpful"

Exclusions for this provider:
- No pharmacotherapy recommendations (not a prescriber)
- No psychological testing (refer to psychologist if needed)
- No couples therapy (individual authorization only)
materials.5:
CASE CONCEPTUALIZATION DRAFT (Fictional Client: "Alex W.")

Presenting Problem:
Client presents with trauma symptoms (nightmares, hypervigilance) and alcohol use (4-5 drinks daily, up from occasional social drinking). Reports increased use since deployment 18 months ago. Meets criteria for both PTSD and Alcohol Use Disorder, moderate.

Draft Conceptualization:
"Client experienced combat trauma during deployment. The trauma led to PTSD symptoms, and the client uses alcohol to cope with the nightmares and hyperarousal. Treatment should focus on processing the trauma, which will likely resolve the drinking."

Supervisor Feedback Needed On:
- Is the formulation too linear/simplistic?
- Are there missing factors (pre-military history, attachment, biological)?
- Is the treatment sequencing appropriate (trauma first vs. substance use first)?
- What theoretical framework best fits this presentation?
- Are there safety considerations being minimized?
materials.6:
ORIGINAL PROGRESS NOTE

"Client attended session and discussed anxiety. Therapist provided supportive counseling. Client reports feeling somewhat better. Will continue treatment."

ACTUAL SESSION FACTS:
- Client: Priya K., Session #9, 50 minutes
- Reported panic attack at work on Tuesday (first in 3 weeks)
- Trigger: Email from manager about upcoming presentation
- Used diaphragmatic breathing in the moment — partially effective (SUDS 8→5)
- Session focus: Cognitive restructuring of catastrophic thoughts about presentation
- Identified automatic thought: "If I stumble, everyone will think I'm incompetent"
- Challenged with evidence: 3 successful presentations this year, positive peer feedback
- Assigned graduated exposure homework: practice presentation to partner, then to one colleague
- GAD-7 administered: 9 (down from 11 last session, 16 at intake)
- Risk assessment: No SI/HI, no safety concerns
- Treatment Goal #2 (Reduce avoidance of work-related stressors): Making progress
materials.7:
IOP PROGRAM CONTEXT

Target population: Adults 18+ with treatment-resistant depression (failed 2+ adequate medication trials or 1+ course of evidence-based psychotherapy without adequate response)

Program structure:
- 4 weeks, 3 days/week, 3 hours/day
- Maximum 10 participants per cohort
- Modalities: CBT for depression, behavioral activation groups, mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT), psychoeducation, individual therapy (1x/week)

Staffing: 1 licensed psychologist (program director), 2 licensed therapists, 1 psychiatric consultant (medication review), 1 case manager

Outcome measures: PHQ-9 (weekly), BDI-II (intake/discharge), WHO-DAS 2.0 (functioning), client satisfaction survey

Accreditation requirements: Must meet CARF Behavioral Health standards

Exclusions: Active psychosis, active substance dependence requiring detox, acute suicidality requiring inpatient level of care

Evidence base: Program modalities should reference published RCTs or meta-analyses
materials.8:
REFERRAL PACKET (Fictional Client: "Devin L.")

Referral Source: County Psychiatric Emergency Services
Date of ED Visit: Last Thursday
Reason for visit: Suicidal ideation with plan (overdose), brought in by roommate

Psychiatric Emergency Note (excerpt):
"28-year-old non-binary individual presented with SI with plan. Reported stockpiling medications over 2 weeks. Denied intent at time of evaluation. Roommate removed medications from home. Patient contracted for safety, declined voluntary admission. Discharged with safety plan and referral for outpatient therapy. Started on Lexapro 10mg."

Self-Report Measures (completed in ED):
- PHQ-9: 22 (Severe)
- Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale: Ideation with plan, no attempt
- PCL-5: 28 (below clinical cutoff)
- AUDIT: 14 (Hazardous drinking)

Brief History (from intake paperwork):
- Previous attempt: Age 19 (overdose, hospitalized 3 days)
- Psychiatric history: Depression since age 16, anxiety
- Current stressors: Job loss 2 months ago, breakup 3 weeks ago, financial stress
- Protective factors: Supportive roommate, engaged with treatment, future-oriented statements about career goals
- Family history: Mother with bipolar disorder, father with alcohol use disorder
- Current medications: Lexapro 10mg (started 5 days ago)
materials.9:
CLIENT STATEMENTS FOR COGNITIVE DISTORTION IDENTIFICATION

1. "My therapist didn't smile when I walked in — she must be angry at me for canceling last week."

2. "I got a B+ on my exam. I'm such a failure."

3. "I should be able to handle this without therapy. Other people deal with worse things."

4. "If I tell my partner how I really feel, they'll leave me. I just know it."

5. "Everything was fine until I moved to this city. Now nothing goes right."

6. "My coworker got promoted instead of me. I'll never advance in my career."

7. "I feel anxious, so something bad must be about to happen."

COGNITIVE DISTORTION CATEGORIES (Beck, Burns):
- All-or-Nothing Thinking
